title: What if a city could drink the rain?
During a storm, water runs across roads and sidewalks.
It carries dirt and oil toward street drains.
When too much water comes at once, streets may flood.
But there is another way to handle rain.
Hard surfaces are part of the problem.
In a forest, soil and plants take in rain.
In a city, roofs and roads stop much of the water from entering the ground.
So water moves faster into drains and rivers.
This moving water is called runoff.
One answer is green infrastructure.
This means using plants and special surfaces to manage rain.
A rain garden may look like a flower bed.
But it sits lower than the ground around it.
It collects water and lets some of it enter the soil.
Some roads and parking areas use special pavement.
This pavement lets water pass through.
Stone under the surface can hold rain for a short time.
Some water enters the ground, and extra water may go into pipes.
Plants on roofs can also catch and hold rain.
These changes can do more than reduce water on streets.
Rain can carry oil, trash, and other pollution.
Gardens and soil can help filter some of it.
Trees can also make city streets cooler.
A small green space can have several jobs.
But green spaces cannot stop every flood.
During a very strong storm, too much rain may fall.
Good design and regular care are important.
Cities still need drains and pipes for extra water.
Experts study how these systems can work together.
Next time it rains, look around your neighborhood.
You may see a garden beside a road or special pavement in a parking lot.
It may be helping water move more slowly.
A city cannot control the rain.
But it can make more room for it.
Make more room for rain.
